patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Kemal Yilmaz is a 61-year-old right-handed man with a complex neurological history who presents to the emergency department with acute worsening of speech, progressive somnolence, inability to walk, and new-onset fever over the past 48 hours. His wife reports that approximately eight months ago he was hospitalized for progressive headaches, slowed speech, gait unsteadiness, and generalized weakness. At that time, extensive workup was undertaken including brain imaging and lumbar puncture. His initial cerebrospinal fluid analysis reportedly showed a predominantly lymphocytic pleocytosis with elevated protein and low glucose. Workup for tuberculosis, lymphoma, paraneoplastic syndromes, and fungal infection were all reported as negative. Imaging at that time revealed small scattered gliotic lesions and some leptomeningeal enhancement, as well as acute ischemic lesions in the right caudate nucleus and left internal capsule, for which aspirin was initiated. Cerebral angiography showed hypoplastic vascular segments but no definitive vasculitis. Despite the inconclusive findings, a presumptive diagnosis of central nervous system vasculitis was made. He was treated with a 7-day intravenous methylprednisolone pulse followed by oral prednisolone taper, and received one dose of cyclophosphamide approximately 10 days prior to this current presentation. He had shown modest improvement after the initial steroid course but never returned to his baseline neurological function, continuing to have mild dysarthria and requiring a cane to walk. Over the past two days, his wife noticed rapid deterioration: his speech became nearly unintelligible, he became increasingly drowsy and difficult to arouse, and he could no longer stand even with assistance. Yesterday evening she measured his temperature at 38.3 degrees Celsius. He had no clear response to acetaminophen. This morning he was minimally responsive, prompting her to call emergency services. She specifically denies any seizure-like activity, urinary incontinence, or recent falls. She notes that his diabetes control has been poor since starting steroids, with home blood glucose readings frequently above 250 mg/dL. He has not had recent sick contacts or known exposures. The clinical team is concerned about the possibility of an infectious complication in the setting of recent immunosuppressive therapy, but the prior history of presumed vasculitis and ischemic strokes creates diagnostic uncertainty.

results.title: Infections in patients receiving immunosuppressive therapy for autoimmune diseases
results.authors: Falagas ME, Manta KG, et al.
results.key_finding: Patients receiving corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide have significantly increased risk of bacterial infections, including invasive pneumococcal disease. Risk increases with higher corticosteroid doses and concurrent lymphopenia.

results.title: Community-acquired bacterial meningitis in adults: an update
results.authors: van de Beek D, Brouwer MC, et al.
results.key_finding: Immunocompromised patients with bacterial meningitis have higher mortality rates and may present atypically. Empiric coverage should include Listeria (ampicillin) in addition to standard ceftriaxone plus vancomycin in patients over 50 or immunocompromised.

results.title: IDSA Practice Guidelines for Bacterial Meningitis 2004
results.authors: Tunkel AR, Hartman BJ, et al.
results.key_finding: For immunocompromised adults, empiric therapy should include ampicillin 2g IV q4h in addition to ceftriaxone and vancomycin, to cover Listeria monocytogenes. Adjunctive dexamethasone is recommended for suspected pneumococcal meningitis.

output.summary: Immunocompromised patients, particularly those on corticosteroids and cytotoxic agents, are at significantly increased risk for bacterial meningitis, including infections with Listeria monocytogenes and other opportunistic pathogens. Empiric regimens for bacterial meningitis in immunosuppressed adults typically include ampicillin in addition to vancomycin and a third-generation cephalosporin to provide Listeria coverage. Adjunctive dexamethasone is recommended in suspected pneumococcal meningitis; its use in severely immunocompromised patients is less well-studied. Outcomes of bacterial meningitis in immunocompromised hosts are generally worse than in immunocompetent adults.

useless_tools.rationale: No evidence of endocarditis as a primary source in this case; echocardiography is not part of routine meningitis workup.
No arrhythmia indication; continuous cardiac monitoring contributes nothing to meningitis diagnosis or treatment.
PET imaging has no role in acute meningitis diagnosis; CT and MRI cover the indications.
Amyloid PET is a dementia biomarker tool with no role in acute infectious meningitis.

sequence_constraints.reason: Per IDSA 2004, non-contrast CT head must precede lumbar puncture whenever any imaging-first criterion is present (altered mental status, focal neurological deficit, papilledema, recent seizure, immunocompromise, or age >60). LP performed in undetected mass effect can precipitate fatal herniation.

Blood cultures must be drawn (under interpret_labs) before the first dose of empiric antibiotics so that culture yield is not lost; in practice this means peripheral cultures are collected at the same draw as the CSF analysis is initiated, and the lab tube sequencing prevents antibiotic exposure before specimen acquisition.

critical_actions: Administer the first dose of empiric IV antibiotics (vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg + ceftriaxone 2 g) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion; do NOT delay antibiotics for LP or imaging beyond what is strictly needed for safety.
Give adjunctive dexamethasone 10 mg IV before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue q6h for 4 days in confirmed pneumococcal meningitis.
Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose.
Obtain CT head before LP because imaging-first criteria are present (altered mental status, immunocompromise, focal signs, papilledema, or age >60).
Send full CSF panel (cell count, differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, meningitis multiplex PCR, lactate) at the LP.
Reassess and de-escalate antibiotics based on Gram stain, culture, and susceptibility results.
Place patient on droplet precautions until meningococcal disease is excluded.
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT delay empiric antimicrobial therapy while awaiting imaging or LP results when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.
Do NOT perform lumbar puncture before CT head when any imaging-first criterion (altered mental status, focal deficit, papilledema, seizure, immunocompromise, age >60) is present.

Do NOT discontinue dexamethasone solely because the Gram stain is negative — completion of the 4-day course is appropriate in suspected pneumococcal meningitis until alternative organism is identified.
Do NOT rely on a negative Gram stain or a 'normal CT' to rule out bacterial meningitis when the clinical syndrome is present.
Do NOT treat with oral antibiotics alone; CNS penetration is inadequate for meningitis.
key_reasoning_points: Acute bacterial meningitis presents with fever, headache, meningismus, and altered mental status; the full triad is present in only ~40%, so partial syndromes warrant aggressive workup.
Antibiotic timing matters: every hour of delay after the first hour increases mortality. Antibiotics MUST precede imaging or LP if either would delay treatment >60 minutes.
CT before LP is mandated when any imaging-first criterion is present (altered mental status, focal signs, papilledema, recent seizure, immunocompromise, or age >60).
Adjunctive dexamethasone (10 mg IV q6h × 4 days) given BEFORE or WITH the first antibiotic dose reduces mortality and unfavourable outcomes in pneumococcal meningitis (De Gans 2002, NEJM).
A negative CSF Gram stain (sensitivity ~60-90%, lower if antibiotic pretreated) does not exclude bacterial meningitis; multiplex PCR or antigen testing retains sensitivity.
CSF:serum glucose ratio <0.4 is more reliable than absolute CSF glucose for distinguishing bacterial from viral meningitis.
Empiric coverage must include vancomycin + ceftriaxone in adults; add ampicillin for Listeria coverage if age >50 or immunocompromised.

metadata.difficulty_description: Moderate - patient with complex prior neurological history including presumed CNS vasculitis and recent immunosuppressive therapy now presenting with acute bacterial meningitis. The prior diagnosis of vasculitis creates diagnostic anchoring bias, steroid use confounds interpretation of inflammatory markers and WBC, and the mixed CSF pleocytosis requires careful interpretation. Multiple comorbidities (diabetes, CKD) add management complexity.
